title: Machine-learning denoising exposes strong size scaling in deep-earthquake rupture parameters
summary: A multitask neural denoiser recovered teleseismic P-wave pulses from deep Mw 5.0+ earthquakes that had previously been too noisy for source analysis. The study found moment–duration scaling M₀ ∼ τ⁴, stress-drop scaling Δσ ∼ M₀⁰·²¹ and radiated-energy scaling Eᵣ ∼ M₀¹·²⁴; deep events had a median radiation efficiency near 5%, weak directivity and few subevents. After accounting for rigidity, no systematic depth trend in duration, stress drop or radiated energy remained across 100–700 km.
ai_technology: DenoTe, a transfer-learned multitask convolutional encoder–decoder neural network
organization: University of Washington, Department of Earth and Space Sciences

evidence.tested: A multitask neural denoiser recovered teleseismic P-wave pulses from deep Mw 5.0+ earthquakes that had previously been too noisy for source analysis.
evidence.unknown: The study is a source-parameter reanalysis enabled by neural denoising, not prospective earthquake prediction. It reports scaling relations and interpretations from the available global event sample; stress and energy estimates remain subject to waveform, path-correction and source-model uncertainties.
evidence.ai_role: Separated low-SNR teleseismic P-wave signals from overlapping noise, enabling source-parameter estimation from 920 deep-earthquake records, including moderate events ordinarily omitted from these analyses.
